answer.question: What should a historic Fernandina Beach property check before turf?
answer.answer: Confirm whether the parcel is in a City historic district and ask preservation staff what review applies to the proposed site change. A Certificate of Appropriateness may be required. Bring the property plan and requirements before finalizing a layout around trees, paths and existing site features.

blocks.h2: Keep the features that give the yard its character.
paras: A small lawn or practice green can sit beside existing paths and planting. Choose useful putting lines or the route a pet area needs, then leave the rest of the landscape intact. On a shallow back yard, walking room can matter more than extra cups.
Mark mature tree canopy and roots before discussing preparation. Resolve any required tree advice early and include leaf cleanup in the care routine.

blocks.h2: Check the proposed change before the outline is final.
paras: Fernandina Beach’s historic districts have a review process for changes to site features. Downtown and Old Town should be checked against the applicable current guidelines rather than treated as one set of rules. Ask staff what the proposal must include and retain the written response.

Outside historic review, applicable City and property requirements still matter. Ask how the proposed turf and base count toward lot coverage, and bring known wet areas or shoreline conditions into the estimate separately from surface selection.

blocks.h2: In the historic district, a new lawn needs a Certificate of Appropriateness.
paras: The Victorian, Queen Anne and frame vernacular houses around Centre Street sit inside a city historic district. There, changing a site feature takes a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic District Council: staff sign off smaller work, and larger work goes to a hearing before the full council (City of Fernandina Beach).

Pools and hardscape already need site plan approval, to protect the district's historic lot patterns and mature landscaping. The council works from guidelines based on the U.S. Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation (downtown design guidelines). Old Town, the Spanish plat of 1811, has its own set, now being rewritten with residents' input (Fernandina Observer).

So plan a layout that keeps the old lot pattern and reads as lawn from the street. Ours is custom and you approve it before work starts, which gives you a drawing to take to the city. Since 19 May 2026, state law has also kept cities from prohibiting compliant turf at a single-family home (Fla. Stat. 125.572). Ask preservation staff how that fits the certificate before you commit to a plan.

blocks.h2: Live oaks old enough to have names, and grass that can't live under them.
paras: Some of the shade here is famous. The Bailey House, built in 1885 at Ash and 7th, has Kate's Tree, and the Lesesne House on Centre Street, from 1860, keeps a live oak about two centuries old (Amelia Island). St. Augustine grass fails under canopy like that, and new sod gets no more light than the old.

The ground under those trees is hard work too: a century of compacted fill and shell on the old lots, root plates you can't trench through, and low back corners that stay wet after a summer storm. We check it on the free visit, prepare the site, and fit the base to what's there, roots included.

The canopy pays you back once turf is down. Shaded turf runs far cooler underfoot than turf in open sun (how hot turf gets), so a yard under the oaks stays kinder to bare feet and paws than an open one.

blocks.h2: Island sand, wetter toward the river, and a code that counts the base.
paras: Fernandina Beach sits at the north end of Amelia Island, the southernmost of the Sea Islands, on barrier-island sand. Nassau County's comprehensive plan describes the island as poorly drained on its west side, along the river and marsh, and better drained on the higher sand (Nassau County). The same plan names the county's wider problem: flat ground and a lot of poorly drained soil.
That's why rain has to go down through the base and away, never toward the house or onto the lot next door. Your base gets built for that soil, with the low corner in mind.

The city counts what's under the turf. Its Land Development Code defines an impervious surface as one compacted or covered so it's highly resistant to infiltration by water, caps impervious cover by land use, and never mentions artificial turf (Fernandina Beach LDC). Ask Planning in writing how they'll count your base before the layout is final, and see our guide to whether turf counts as impervious.

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Fernandina Beach, FL?
faq.a: We install artificial turf, pet turf and backyard putting greens in Fernandina Beach, FL. Inside the historic district, work on site features needs a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic District Council, so plan the layout with that in mind. Under the old live oaks, turf gives you the green that shaded grass never keeps. Call 303-349-2368 for a free estimate.

faq.q: Is my house in Fernandina Beach's historic district?
faq.a: Check the city's historic districts page before you plan (City of Fernandina Beach). The National Register district was listed in 1973 at about 1,500 acres and grew by 970 acres in 1987 (Wikipedia). If you're inside a city district, the Certificate of Appropriateness comes first.

faq.q: Can I put a putting green in a historic-district back yard?
faq.a: Usually, yes: a small practice green suits the shallow back yards here. Show it on the plan you take to the city, like any other site feature. For the full game, the city owns the 27-hole Fernandina Beach Golf Club on Bill Melton Road (Destination Amelia).

faq.q: Can an HOA stop turf outside the historic district?
faq.a: HOAs are common on the newer streets and in the gated golf communities. An association can't restrict turf that's hidden from the frontage, the lots next door, common areas and any community golf course (Fla. Stat. 720.3045). For anything the street can see, put the plan in front of the board first.

faq.q: If I re-sod the shady patch, how often can I water it?
faq.a: Under the Phase III order, new plantings get daily watering for 15 days, then three days a week for 30 days, then two days a week for 15 more (St. Johns River Water Management District). After that it's one day a week like the rest of the lawn, under the same shade that thinned the last sod.
